1298: The effect of location on the arginine content of freshly harvested grain was non-significant, the three locations returning closely comparable values: Birbhum/Howrah recorded 0.3113 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.3110 mg/100 mg and Nadia 0.3100 mg/100 mg.
1300: The landraces differed distinctly, the varietal effect being highly significant. Gobindabhog ranked highest with 0.4205 mg/100 mg, Radhunipagal occupied second position at 0.3102 mg/100 mg and Kalojira the last at 0.2016 mg/100 mg.
1302: Location and variety did not interact significantly, indicating uniform landrace behaviour across the three locations. The highest single combination was Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah with 0.4223 mg/100 mg and the lowest Kalojira at Nadia with 0.1985 mg/100 mg. Since the determination was confined to fresh grain, storage terms do not arise.
1311: Arginine is conditionally essential: healthy adults synthesise it in sufficient quantity, whereas infants and individuals under physiological stress do not. It assists in the disposal of waste nitrogen and is required for the synthesis of nitric oxide, a vasodilator. The three locations differed by only 0.0013 mg/100 mg and the effect was non-significant, Birbhum and Howrah returning 0.3113 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.3110 and Nadia 0.3100. Gobindabhog contained 0.4205 mg/100 mg, more than double the 0.2016 of Kalojira, with Radhunipagal intermediate at 0.3102 mg/100 mg. Arginine is concentrated in the embryo and the outer layers of the grain, so the milling behaviour of each landrace will condition the proportion surviving into the polished rice. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) listed arginine among the amino acids abundant in the prolamin fraction of rice.

1317: Marked differences emerged between landraces, the varietal effect being highly significant. Gobindabhog ranked highest at 0.5587 mg/100 mg, followed by Radhunipagal at 0.3886 mg/100 mg, with Kalojira lowest at 0.2804 mg/100 mg.

Storage was not sampled for this character, so no term involving it is reported.
1328: Glycine is the smallest and structurally simplest amino acid. It constitutes a major component of collagen and assists hepatic detoxification. The three locations were separated by 0.0012 mg/100 mg, a non-significant margin, Nadia returning 0.4098 mg/100 mg, Purba Bardhaman 0.4092 and Birbhum and Howrah 0.4086. Gobindabhog contained 0.5587 mg/100 mg against 0.2804 in Kalojira, almost exactly double, with Radhunipagal at 0.3886 mg/100 mg. The doubling observed alike for glycine, serine and histidine suggests a general difference in the quantity of storage protein rather than any distinctive feature of an individual amino acid. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) reported glycine among the amino acids abundant in the prolamin fraction, and Kamjijam et al. (2020) localised it to the germ and outer layers of the rice grain.

1334: The three landraces differed distinctly, the varietal effect attaining the 1% level. Gobindabhog carried the highest quantity, 0.6690 mg/100 mg, followed by Radhunipagal at 0.5183 mg/100 mg, with the lowest quantity recorded in Kalojira at 0.4526 mg/100 mg.

1345: Aspartic acid is a non-essential amino acid participating in the urea cycle and in cellular energy pathways; together with glutamic acid it contributes to the savoury character of cooked food. The three locations lay within 0.0005 mg/100 mg of one another and the effect was non-significant. The coefficient of variation, at 1.37%, was the second lowest of all fifteen amino acids, attesting to the repeatability of the determination. The spread between landraces was narrower here than for most other amino acids: Gobindabhog contained 0.6690 mg/100 mg, Radhunipagal 0.5183 and Kalojira 0.4526, Gobindabhog thus exceeding Kalojira by 48% rather than by the doubling observed elsewhere. Kamjijam et al. (2020) localised aspartic acid to the germ of the rice grain and identified it among the amino acids present in the greatest quantity.

1362: Glutamic acid was the most abundant amino acid in all three landraces. It is the principal amino acid of cereal storage protein and confers much of the savoury character of cooked rice. The three locations differed by only 0.0010 mg/100 mg, a non-significant margin, and the coefficient of variation, at 0.64%, was the lowest of all the amino acids. As glutamic acid constitutes the mainstay of the glutelin fraction, its proportion cannot vary greatly from one landrace to another. Renuka et al. (2022) demonstrated that it operates in conjunction with proline and ornithine as a precursor of 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline. The extremes were Gobindabhog at Birbhum and Howrah with 1.4694 mg/100 mg and Kalojira at the same location with 1.1130 mg/100 mg, which indicates that landrace was determinative and location was not.

1379: Threonine is an essential amino acid required for the synthesis of protective intestinal mucin and of immunoglobulins, and after lysine it is frequently the amino acid in shortest supply in cereal-based diets. The three locations lay within 0.0001 mg/100 mg of one another and the effect was non-significant. Gobindabhog contained 0.2770 mg/100 mg, twice the 0.1368 recorded in Kalojira, with Radhunipagal at 0.1898 mg/100 mg. As threonine is one of the limiting amino acids in a rice-based diet, a doubling between landraces carries genuine nutritional import and distinguishes Gobindabhog for any selection made on protein quality. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) reported the threonine content of rice protein as 3.15 to 4.43% and listed threonine, with lysine and tryptophan, among the amino acids in shortest supply in rice.

1396: Alanine is a non-essential amino acid that transports nitrogen from the musculature to the liver and participates in the cycle converting protein to glucose under conditions of energy demand. The three locations were separated by 0.0019 mg/100 mg, a non-significant margin. Gobindabhog contained 0.6596 mg/100 mg against 0.2739 in Kalojira, a difference of 141% and the widest relative margin of any amino acid other than cysteine and tyrosine, with Radhunipagal at 0.4171 mg/100 mg. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) characterised the amino acid balance of rice as uneven, alanine ranking among the amino acids present in the greatest quantity at 4 to 11% of the total, much of it residing in the prolamin fraction. The interaction was non-significant and the ranking was conserved throughout.

1413: Proline merits particular attention in a study of aromatic rice. Beyond its structural role in protein, it is the compound from which the plant synthesises 2-acetyl-1-pyrroline, the substance responsible for the characteristic fragrance of aromatic rice. This ranking warrants scrutiny, since it runs counter to the aroma scores, in which Kalojira ranked first by a wide margin and Gobindabhog second. Luo et al. (2020) demonstrated this directly. The two measures need not therefore correspond, and the result serves as a caution that a high total proline content does not of itself guarantee a fragrant grain. Itani et al. (2004) attributed such locational differences in aroma to the quantity of precursor available to the grain during filling, and Imran et al. (2023) reviewed the recent work on this pathway.

1430: Cysteine carries a sulphur group, which distinguishes it from the other amino acids determined here. Kalojira accordingly contained nearly a thousand times more cysteine than Radhunipagal. This finding should be verified against the raw chromatograms before the table is finalised, since a failure to detect a peak is indistinguishable from a genuine absence. Jayaprakash et al. (2022) reported cysteine in rice protein over a range of 0.13 to 3.42%, so a landrace difference of this order is not implausible. The elevated cysteine of Kalojira is consistent with its standing as the landrace of greatest antioxidant capacity, the sulphur group contributing to that property. Cysteine is the amino acid forming the sulphur bridges responsible for the declining solubility of protein as rice ages (Chrastil and Zarins, 1992), which suggests that Kalojira may be the landrace most susceptible to that change during protracted storage.
